title: It Was in Vogue
paragraphs: The comic script that follows explains that many a word found in the dictionary is not in use today, and a few of them have completely disappeared. Look at the verse below:
> Mōttai, takar, uṭal and appar > Designate the male sheep.

In Aṇṇā’s play Nīti Tēvaṉ Mayakkam, Rāvaṇaṉ files a case against Kampar. He takes umbrage at Kampar describing him as “a merciless demon” in his version of Rāmāyaṇa and he himself argues his case before the judge.

“I didn’t even touch Cīta, and safeguarded her in the garden of Ashoka. Juxtapose my chivalry with Intira’s who raped Akalya, Cantiraṉ who raped his teacher’s wife, Lakcumaṇaṉ who chopped off the nose and breast of Cūrpaṇakai, Lord Civa who misbehaved with the wives of the sages in Tārukāvaṇam and Rāma, who assailed Vāli hidden from a vantage point. How could I be termed merciless?” This is Rāvaṇaṉ’s defence.
The judge, out of his inability to pass a judgement against the gods, faints.
In the same manner, here comes another piece of imagination. Appar, Campantar, Cuntarar and Māṇikkavācakar were the four renowned Caiva devotees. They were also great poets in Tamil.

Among them, Tirunāvukkaracar who was known as Appar brings a case before the judge. His contention is that his name included under non-human beings (akṟiṇai) in Marapiyal of Tolkāppiyam must be deleted.

The judge observes, “It doesn’t seem that Tolkāppiyar included your name wantonly to denigrate your reputation, since Tolkāppiyar lived in an era much before that of yours. How could he contemplate maligning your name as you live in a later period?
“I accept your explanation regarding difference in the era. Therefore, I do not indict Tolkāppiyar personally. It would be enough if my name be deleted.”
The judge passes the judgement ordering that the name of Appar be deleted.
Therefore, the term appar grouped with mōttai, takar, uṭal ceased to be there in the list.
Thus was the word appar that meant a he-goat made to disappear from the list.
The account above is only an imaginary, humorous anecdote.
Pērāciriyar, the commentator, points out that the convention of using the word appar for a he-goat fell out of use in later years.
